claim: Recent work has revealed a principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity capturing the separation of sensory-motor cortex from transmodal regions of the default mode network (DMN).
source: Recent work has revealed a principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity capturing the separation of sensory-motor cortex from transmodal regions of the default mode network (DMN); this is thought to facilitate memory-guided cognition.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Margulies et al., 2016) establishing the principal gradient.

claim: The principal gradient is thought to facilitate memory-guided cognition.
source: Recent work has revealed a principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity capturing the separation of sensory-motor cortex from transmodal regions of the default mode network (DMN); this is thought to facilitate memory-guided cognition.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation cited from prior literature.

claim: Multivoxel activation patterns at opposite ends of the principal gradient were more divergent when participants retrieved stronger associations.
source: Multivoxel activation patterns at opposite ends of the principal gradient were more divergent when participants retrieved stronger associations; therefore, when long-term semantic information is sufficient for ongoing cognition, regions supporting heteromodal memory are functionally separated from sensory-motor experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the gradient decomposition analysis comparing strong and weak associations.

claim: When long-term semantic information is sufficient for ongoing cognition, regions supporting heteromodal memory are functionally separated from sensory-motor experience.
source: Multivoxel activation patterns at opposite ends of the principal gradient were more divergent when participants retrieved stronger associations; therefore, when long-term semantic information is sufficient for ongoing cognition, regions supporting heteromodal memory are functionally separated from sensory-motor experience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding gradient divergence during strong association retrieval.

claim: When less related concepts were linked, the dimension of connectivity was reduced in strength as semantic control regions separated from the DMN to generate more flexible and original responses.
source: In contrast, when less related concepts were linked, this dimension of connectivity was reduced in strength as semantic control regions separated from the DMN to generate more flexible and original responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced gradient values for weak associations in semantic control regions.

claim: There were fewer dimensions within the neural response towards the apex of the principal gradient when strong associations were retrieved.
source: We also observed fewer dimensions within the neural response towards the apex of the principal gradient when strong associations were retrieved, reflecting less complex or varied neural coding across trials and participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dimensionality analysis using PCA on neural activation patterns.

claim: Fewer dimensions in neural response towards the apex of the principal gradient reflect less complex or varied neural coding across trials and participants.
source: We also observed fewer dimensions within the neural response towards the apex of the principal gradient when strong associations were retrieved, reflecting less complex or varied neural coding across trials and participants.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dimensionality findings.

claim: The separation of DMN from sensory-motor systems is a hallmark of the retrieval of strong conceptual links that are culturally shared.
source: In this way, the principal gradient explains how semantic cognition is organised in the human cerebral cortex: the separation of DMN from sensory-motor systems is a hallmark of the retrieval of strong conceptual links that are culturally shared.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental findings regarding gradient separation and behavioral data on shared meanings.

claim: The principal gradient is the dimension of intrinsic connectivity that typically explains the most variance in whole-brain decompositions of human resting-state fMRI data.
source: This principal gradient is the dimension of intrinsic connectivity that typically explains the most variance in whole-brain decompositions of human resting-state fMRI data (Hong et al., 2020, Huntenburg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The principal gradient is correlated with physical distance along the cortical mantle from primary sensory-motor landmarks.
source: It is correlated with physical distance along the cortical mantle from primary sensory-motor landmarks.
evidence: This is a known property of the principal gradient from prior literature.

claim: The principal gradient captures the order of large-scale networks in frontal, temporal, and parietal regions showing transitions from sensory-motor regions, through attention networks to frontoparietal control and then default mode network (DMN) regions.
source: It captures the order of large-scale networks in frontal, temporal, and parietal regions – all of which show transitions from sensory-motor regions, through attention networks to frontoparietal control and then default mode network (DMN) regions.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization captured by the principal gradient, based on prior literature.

claim: Opposing ends of the principal gradient are implicated in sensory and memory-based decisions.
source: It also captures functional transitions: for instance, opposing ends of the principal gradient are implicated in sensory and memory-based decisions (Murphy et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2018; Lanzoni et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The principal gradient supports increasingly abstract levels of representation, allowing heteromodal regions in the DMN to take on roles that are less directly influenced by externally driven neural activity.
source: Theories suggest the principal gradient supports increasingly abstract levels of representation, allowing heteromodal regions in the DMN to take on roles that are less directly influenced by externally driven neural activity (Smallwood et al., 2021; Margulies et al., 2016; Huntenburg et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The representations of events extracted from movie-watching data vary in length along the principal gradient hierarchy, with short events represented in sensory areas and longer events in transmodal regions including within the default mode network.
source: In line with this account, the representations of events extracted from movie-watching data are thought to vary in length along this hierarchy, with short events represented in sensory areas and longer events in transmodal regions including within the default mode network (Baldassano et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Semantic representation draws on both ends of the principal gradient.
source: Semantic representation is thought to draw on both ends of this principal gradient (Huth et al., 2016; Barsalou, 2008; Kiefer and Pulvermüller, 2012; Meteyard et al., 2012; Patterson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2010; Visser and Lambon Ralph, 2011; Murphy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The graded hub and spoke model proposes that heteromodal concepts are formed at a distance from visual and auditory input regions.
source: The graded hub and spoke model proposes that heteromodal concepts are formed at a distance from visual and auditory input regions: diverse sensory processing pathways gradually converge in transmodal areas to form abstract generalisable semantic representations (Patterson et al., 2007; Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from prior literature.

claim: Diverse sensory processing pathways gradually converge in transmodal areas to form abstract generalisable semantic representations.
source: The graded hub and spoke model proposes that heteromodal concepts are formed at a distance from visual and auditory input regions: diverse sensory processing pathways gradually converge in transmodal areas to form abstract generalisable semantic representations (Patterson et al., 2007; Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is part of the graded hub and spoke model from prior literature.

claim: Flexible deployment of conceptual information involves the recruitment of several heteromodal networks, including the DMN, semantic control network (SCN) and multiple-demand network (MDN), which lie at different points along the principal gradient.
source: Moreover, we flexibly deploy conceptual information to suit our goals or context: this involves the recruitment of several heteromodal networks, including the DMN, semantic control network (SCN) and multiple-demand network (MDN), which lie at different points along the principal gradient (Wang et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Higher conceptual overlap is associated with stronger activation at the top end of the principal gradient.
source: These networks show differential recruitment across trials depending on the semantic similarity of the items being linked, with higher conceptual overlap associated with stronger activation at the top end of the principal gradient (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Anterior temporal lobe (ATL) and angular gyrus (AG) contribute to the relatively automatic retrieval of semantic information strongly supported by long-term memory.
source: Anterior temporal lobe (ATL) and angular gyrus (AG), which are allied with DMN, contribute to the relatively automatic retrieval of semantic information strongly supported by long-term memory (Davey et al., 2015; Jefferies et al., 2020, Teige et al., 2019; Teige et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: When unusual aspects of knowledge are required, there is greater recruitment of the SCN to shape the meaning that is retrieved.
source: In contrast, when unusual aspects of knowledge are required – for example, for weak associations – there is greater recruitment of the SCN to shape the meaning that is retrieved (Davey et al., 2015; Jackson, 2021; Jefferies, 2013; Jefferies et al., 2020), along with other control regions within the MDN, which responds to higher task demands across domains (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Erb et al., 2013; Assem et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The MDN responds to higher task demands across domains.
source: In contrast, when unusual aspects of knowledge are required – for example, for weak associations – there is greater recruitment of the SCN to shape the meaning that is retrieved (Davey et al., 2015; Jackson, 2021; Jefferies, 2013; Jefferies et al., 2020), along with other control regions within the MDN, which responds to higher task demands across domains (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Erb et al., 2013; Assem et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Visual object recognition is supported by a processing hierarchy extending from primary visual cortex, through higher visual regions in inferior temporal cortex, to ventral anterior temporal areas that capture the meaning of concepts across modalities.
source: Visual object recognition is supported by a processing hierarchy extending from primary visual cortex, through higher visual regions in inferior temporal cortex, to ventral anterior temporal areas that capture the meaning of concepts across modalities (Murphy et al., 2017; Ju and Bassett, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Medial temporal cortex supports detailed, fine-grained spatial representations in posterior hippocampus and more gist or schema like, coarse-grained memory representations in anterior hippocampus.
source: A similar functional transition is proposed in medial temporal cortex, which supports detailed, fine-grained spatial representations in posterior hippocampus and more gist or schema like, coarse-grained memory representations in anterior hippocampus (Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Lateral prefrontal cortex supports a rostral–caudal gradient, representing specific motor actions in posterior regions through to more abstract goals in anterior regions.
source: Lateral prefrontal cortex has also been proposed to support a rostral–caudal gradient, representing specific motor actions in posterior regions through to more abstract goals in anterior regions (Badre and D'Esposito, 2009; Badre and Nee, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Neural representation in unimodal regions is thought to have many dimensions, allowing the cortex to discriminate between similar inputs.
source: Neural representation in unimodal regions is thought to have many dimensions, allowing the cortex to discriminate between similar inputs, while the representational space may have fewer dimensions in transmodal DMN regions, allowing a variety of inputs to be encoded into common activity patterns that generalise knowledge across circumstances (Ju and Bassett, 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The representational space may have fewer dimensions in transmodal DMN regions, allowing a variety of inputs to be encoded into common activity patterns that generalise knowledge across circumstances.
source: Neural representation in unimodal regions is thought to have many dimensions, allowing the cortex to discriminate between similar inputs, while the representational space may have fewer dimensions in transmodal DMN regions, allowing a variety of inputs to be encoded into common activity patterns that generalise knowledge across circumstances (Ju and Bassett, 2020).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Category learning based on an abstract rule is associated with a prefrontal response characterised by fewer dimensions.
source: Category learning based on an abstract rule is also associated with a prefrontal response characterised by fewer dimensions (Mack et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Participants' in-scanner ratings of the strength of the link they made between the words in each pair were strongly correlated with word2vec values (Pearson r = 0.84, p < 0.001).
source: Participants' in-scanner ratings of the strength of the link they made between the words in each pair were strongly correlated with word2vec values as expected (Pearson r = 0.84, p < 0.001), see Figure 1C.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There was a significant negative correlation between word2vec and the number of meanings generated (r = −0.53, p < 0.001).
source: There was a significant negative correlation between word2vec and the number of meanings generated (r = −0.53, p < 0.001), confirming that participants generated more variable patterns of semantic retrieval for weakly associated word-pairs, see Figure 1D.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Participants generated more variable patterns of semantic retrieval for weakly associated word-pairs.
source: There was a significant negative correlation between word2vec and the number of meanings generated (r = −0.53, p < 0.001), confirming that participants generated more variable patterns of semantic retrieval for weakly associated word-pairs, see Figure 1D.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between word2vec and number of meanings.

claim: The average reaction time on the chevron task was 0.336 s and the accuracy was 72.6%.
source: On the chevron task, the average reaction time was 0.336 s and the accuracy was 72.6%; these data suggest the task was challenging enough to engage the participant but not so difficult that they could not do it.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral performance data.

claim: The chevron task was challenging enough to engage the participant but not so difficult that they could not do it.
source: On the chevron task, the average reaction time was 0.336 s and the accuracy was 72.6%; these data suggest the task was challenging enough to engage the participant but not so difficult that they could not do it.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral performance data.

claim: The fast pace of the chevron task reduced participants' ability to think about semantic links across trials.
source: The fast pace of this task reduced participants' ability to think about semantic links across trials.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of task design on cognitive processing.

claim: The first gradient from informational connectivity was highly overlapping with the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity identified by prior work (Margulies et al., 2016), for both the semantic and chevron tasks (Spin permutation p value: pspin < 0.001).
source: The first gradient, accounting for the greatest variance in informational connectivity, was highly overlapping with the principal gradient of intrinsic connectivity identified by prior work (Margulies et al., 2016), for both the semantic and chevron tasks (Spin permutation p value: pspin < 0.001), see Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison using spin permutation tests and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gradient which explained the second most variance for the semantic task was positively correlated with the corresponding gradient derived from resting data (pspin < 0.001).
source: The gradient which explained the second most variance for the semantic task was also positively correlated with the corresponding gradient derived from resting data (pspin < 0.001), demonstrating a pattern of distinguishing visual areas from auditory/motor areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis using spin permutation tests.

claim: The second gradient demonstrates a pattern of distinguishing visual areas from auditory/motor areas.
source: The gradient which explained the second most variance for the semantic task was also positively correlated with the corresponding gradient derived from resting data (pspin < 0.001), demonstrating a pattern of distinguishing visual areas from auditory/motor areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial pattern of the second gradient.

claim: The gradient which explained third most variance for the semantic task was only positively correlated with the corresponding gradient derived from resting data in the left hemisphere (pspin < 0.001), while a negative relationship was found for the right hemisphere.
source: The gradient which explained third most variance for the semantic task was only positively correlated with the corresponding gradient derived from resting data in the left hemisphere (pspin < 0.001), while a negative relationship was found for the right hemisphere, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant increase in principal gradient values for strong versus weak associations in transmodal areas implicated in semantic cognition, including in bilateral prefrontal cortex, temporal lobe, and presupplementary motor cortex.
source: This analysis revealed a significant increase in principal gradient values for strong versus weak associations in transmodal areas implicated in semantic cognition, including in bilateral prefrontal cortex, temporal lobe, and presupplementary motor cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gradient decomposition analysis comparing strong and weak associations.

claim: Lower principal gradient values for strong versus weak associations were found in sensory-motor regions towards the bottom of the principal gradient.
source: The reverse of this pattern (i.e. lower principal gradient values for strong versus weak associations) was found in sensory-motor regions towards the bottom of the principal gradient.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gradient decomposition analysis.

claim: There were significant differences in principal gradient values for the semantic task across SCN and SCN + MDN compared with MDN regions.
source: Simple t-tests revealed significant differences in principal gradient values for the semantic task across SCN and SCN + MDN compared with MDN regions (t(30) = 3.259, p = 0.0167, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [0.279 ~1.215], Cohen's d = 0.827; and t(30) = 3.904, p = 0.003, 95% CI = [0.334 ~1.066], Cohen's d = 0.965, respectively), while no significant differences between networks were found for the chevron task (p > 0.682).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-test results with Bonferroni correction.

claim: No significant differences between networks were found for the chevron task (p > 0.682).
source: Simple t-tests revealed significant differences in principal gradient values for the semantic task across SCN and SCN + MDN compared with MDN regions (t(30) = 3.259, p = 0.0167, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [0.279 ~1.215], Cohen's d = 0.827; and t(30) = 3.904, p = 0.003, 95% CI = [0.334 ~1.066], Cohen's d = 0.965, respectively), while no significant differences between networks were found for the chevron task (p > 0.682).
evidence: This claim is supported by t-test results.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the gradient difference value for each parcel (between strong and weak associations) and resting-state gradient for the semantic task (r = 0.369, p < 0.001).
source: There was a positive correlation for the semantic task: parcels higher on the resting-state gradient tended to show a larger effect of associative strength (strong > weak) on task-derived gradient values (r = 0.369, p < 0.001), while no correlation was found in the chevron task (r = −0.038, p = 0.45), see Figure 2E, F.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No correlation was found between gradient difference values and resting-state gradient in the chevron task (r = −0.038, p = 0.45).
source: There was a positive correlation for the semantic task: parcels higher on the resting-state gradient tended to show a larger effect of associative strength (strong > weak) on task-derived gradient values (r = 0.369, p < 0.001), while no correlation was found in the chevron task (r = −0.038, p = 0.45), see Figure 2E, F.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was a significant correlation between the resting-state gradient and the difference of gradient values between strong and weak associations for the semantic response using spin permutation (pspin < 0.001).
source: These results were confirmed using spin permutation to control for the effects of spatial autocorrelation: again, there was a significant correlation between the resting-state gradient and the difference of gradient values between strong and weak associations for the semantic response (pspin < 0.001), while no such effect was found for the chevron task (pspin = 0.195).
evidence: This claim is supported by spin permutation analysis controlling for spatial autocorrelation.

claim: No significant effect was found for the chevron task using spin permutation (pspin = 0.195).
source: These results were confirmed using spin permutation to control for the effects of spatial autocorrelation: again, there was a significant correlation between the resting-state gradient and the difference of gradient values between strong and weak associations for the semantic response (pspin < 0.001), while no such effect was found for the chevron task (pspin = 0.195).
evidence: This claim is supported by spin permutation analysis.

claim: There was a weak negative correlation overall between dimensionality and principal gradient values (r = −0.155, p = 0.0018).
source: The results showed a weak negative correlation overall (when all trials were included) between dimensionality and principal gradient values (r = −0.155, p = 0.0018), suggesting that the dimensionality of neural coding decreased, at least to some extent, along the principal gradient from unimodal to heteromodal regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of dimensionality and gradient values.

claim: The dimensionality of neural coding decreased along the principal gradient from unimodal to heteromodal regions.
source: The results showed a weak negative correlation overall (when all trials were included) between dimensionality and principal gradient values (r = −0.155, p = 0.0018), suggesting that the dimensionality of neural coding decreased, at least to some extent, along the principal gradient from unimodal to heteromodal regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the negative correlation between dimensionality and gradient values.

claim: The magnitude of the negative correlation between dimensionality and principal gradient increased as a function of association strength (r = −0.425, p < 0.001).
source: Importantly, the magnitude of this negative correlation increased as a function of association strength (r = −0.425, p < 0.001, see Figure 3D): more strongly associated word-pairs generated neural responses at the heteromodal end of the gradient which had even lower dimensionality.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: More strongly associated word-pairs generated neural responses at the heteromodal end of the gradient which had even lower dimensionality.
source: Importantly, the magnitude of this negative correlation increased as a function of association strength (r = −0.425, p < 0.001, see Figure 3D): more strongly associated word-pairs generated neural responses at the heteromodal end of the gradient which had even lower dimensionality.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation analysis results.

claim: The pattern of negative correlation between dimensionality and gradient remained significant when regions in limbic network were removed due to their low tSNR (r = −0.346, p = 0.038).
source: This pattern remained significant even when regions in limbic network were removed due to their low tSNR (r = −0.346, p = 0.038).
evidence: This claim is supported by a control analysis excluding limbic regions.

claim: There was a weak negative correlation between overall dimensionality and the principal gradient estimated by resting-state data for the chevron task (r = −0.08, p < 0.001).
source: There was a weak negative corelation between overall dimensionality (averaged across all trials) and the principal gradient estimated by resting-state data (r = −0.08, p < 0.001), in line with the expectation of more abstract representations at the top of the gradient.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis for the chevron task.

claim: The relationship between the resting-state principal gradient and dimensionality did not vary with the association strength of the preceding semantic trial for the chevron task (r = −0.18, p = 0.28).
source: The relationship between the resting-state principal gradient and dimensionality (estimated for sets of four trials with similar strength of association) did not vary with the association strength of the preceding semantic trial (r = −0.18, p = 0.28, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The neural response had significantly higher dimensionality for weakly related trials in regions implicated in semantic control, including inferior frontal gyrus, presupplementary motor cortex, and posterior middle temporal gyrus in the left hemisphere.
source: A direct comparison of weak and strong associations (contrasting the bottom and top third of the trials arranged according to associative strength) revealed that the neural response had significantly higher dimensionality for weakly related trials in regions implicated in semantic control, including inferior frontal gyrus, presupplementary motor cortex, and posterior middle temporal gyrus in the left hemisphere, as well as in regions of the default mode network including the bilateral AG, precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex, and left anterior temporal pole (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct comparison analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The neural response had significantly higher dimensionality for weakly related trials in regions of the default mode network including the bilateral AG, precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex, and left anterior temporal pole.
source: A direct comparison of weak and strong associations (contrasting the bottom and top third of the trials arranged according to associative strength) revealed that the neural response had significantly higher dimensionality for weakly related trials in regions implicated in semantic control, including inferior frontal gyrus, presupplementary motor cortex, and posterior middle temporal gyrus in the left hemisphere, as well as in regions of the default mode network including the bilateral AG, precuneus, medial prefrontal cortex, and left anterior temporal pole (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct comparison analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No clusters showed higher dimensionality for activation patterns during the retrieval of strong associations.
source: No clusters showed the reverse pattern (i.e. higher dimensionality for activation patterns during the retrieval of strong associations).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the dimensionality comparison analysis.

claim: The strongest dimensionality difference was within semantic control areas, with no effect of association strength in multiple-demand areas.
source: Confirmatory analyses examined the effect of association strength on dimensionality in networks defined using resting-state data (Yeo et al., 2011) and functional recruitment during semantic and control tasks. This confirmed the strongest dimensionality difference was within semantic control areas, with no effect of association strength in multiple-demand areas, see Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by network-based analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the dimensionality change across weak and strong associations and the principal gradient value for each parcel obtained from intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.352, p < 0.001).
source: Using Schaefer's 400-region parcellation, we established a significant positive correlation between the dimensionality change across weak and strong associations and the principal gradient value for each parcel obtained from both intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.352, p < 0.001, Figure 3E) and the informational connectivity of our semantic task (r = 0.549, p < 0.001, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between the dimensionality change across weak and strong associations and the principal gradient value for each parcel obtained from the informational connectivity of the semantic task (r = 0.549, p < 0.001).
source: Using Schaefer's 400-region parcellation, we established a significant positive correlation between the dimensionality change across weak and strong associations and the principal gradient value for each parcel obtained from both intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.352, p < 0.001, Figure 3E) and the informational connectivity of our semantic task (r = 0.549, p < 0.001, Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The semantic representational space is more strongly modulated by association strength towards the heteromodal end of the principal gradient.
source: These results show that the semantic representational space is more strongly modulated by association strength towards the heteromodal end of the principal gradient, implicating these regions in individual differences in semantic cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between dimensionality change and gradient values.

claim: Neural pattern similarity was positively associated with semantic similarity in inferior frontal gyrus, posterior middle temporal gyrus, right ATL, bilateral lateral and medial parietal cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, and middle and superior frontal cortex.
source: A semantic similarity matrix, based on the correlation of participants' ratings of associative strength across trials (reflecting the global similarity of neural states of retrieval between participants; left-hand panel of Figure 4A), was positively associated with neural pattern similarity in inferior frontal gyrus, posterior middle temporal gyrus, right ATL, bilateral lateral and medial parietal cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, and middle and superior frontal cortex (right-hand panel of Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by second-order RSA results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Semantic control regions and DMN showed the strongest association with individual differences in associative strength ratings across participants.
source: Functional masks defined by semantic and control tasks and classical resting-state networks (Yeo et al., 2011) confirmed that semantic control regions and DMN showed the strongest association with individual differences in associative strength ratings across participants, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by network-based analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with dimensionality differences between strongly associated and weakly associated trials (r = 0.506, p < 0.001).
source: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with dimensionality differences between strongly associated and weakly associated trials (r = 0.506, p < 0.001, Figure 4C), and with the principal gradient derived from the semantic task (r = 0.42, p < 0.001, Figure 4B) and from intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.255, p < 0.001; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with the principal gradient derived from the semantic task (r = 0.42, p < 0.001).
source: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with dimensionality differences between strongly associated and weakly associated trials (r = 0.506, p < 0.001, Figure 4C), and with the principal gradient derived from the semantic task (r = 0.42, p < 0.001, Figure 4B) and from intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.255, p < 0.001; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with the principal gradient derived from intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.255, p < 0.001).
source: Semantic-brain alignment was positively associated with dimensionality differences between strongly associated and weakly associated trials (r = 0.506, p < 0.001, Figure 4C), and with the principal gradient derived from the semantic task (r = 0.42, p < 0.001, Figure 4B) and from intrinsic connectivity (r = 0.255, p < 0.001; see Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation between the principal gradient and semantic-brain alignment could be partially explained by dimensionality difference (indirect effect: a × b = 0.0053, 95% CI = [0.0039–0.01], p < 0.001, explaining 51.7% variance).
source: Consistent with our prediction, we found the correlation between the principal gradient and semantic-brain alignment could be partially explained by this dimensionality difference (indirect effect: a × b = 0.0053, 95% CI = [0.0039–0.01], p < 0.001, explaining 51.7% variance; direct effect: c′ = 0.0049, 95% CI = [0.0026–0.01], p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by mediation analysis results.

claim: The apex of the principal gradient might relate to individual differences in semantic cognition because its behaviour reflects the extent to which information is common across individuals.
source: This result suggests the apex of the principal gradient might relate to individual differences in semantic cognition because its behaviour reflects the extent to which information is common across individuals: when there is greater semantic-brain alignment at the top of the gradient, the neural patterns for strong associations also show less variation and complexity than for weak associations (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mediation analysis results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The variance explained by the principal gradient was higher for the decomposition of informational connectivity than for time-series correlation (40–50% vs. 25%).
source: Moreover, the variance explained by the principal gradient was higher for the decomposition of informational connectivity than for time-series correlation (40–50% vs. 25%).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of variance explained by different connectivity methods.

claim: In children, the overarching organisational gradient is anchored within the unimodal cortex, between somatosensory/motor and visual territories.
source: One recent study Dong et al., 2021 found that, in children, the overarching organisational gradient is anchored within the unimodal cortex, between somatosensory/motor and visual territories, while in adolescence, the principal gradient of connectivity transitions into an adult-like spatial framework, with the default network at the opposite end of a spectrum from primary sensory and motor regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior developmental study.

claim: In adolescence, the principal gradient of connectivity transitions into an adult-like spatial framework, with the default network at the opposite end of a spectrum from primary sensory and motor regions.
source: One recent study Dong et al., 2021 found that, in children, the overarching organisational gradient is anchored within the unimodal cortex, between somatosensory/motor and visual territories, while in adolescence, the principal gradient of connectivity transitions into an adult-like spatial framework, with the default network at the opposite end of a spectrum from primary sensory and motor regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior developmental study.

claim: There is strong overlap between the semantic network recruited during tasks and DMN regions identified from the parcellation of resting-state data, for example in inferior and lateral temporal and lateral parietal cortices.
